meta.name: Aortic Dissection — Sudden Tearing Chest Pain at the Bank, Bilateral BP Differential, ASA Withheld, Load-and-Go

patient.name: David Clark
patient.chiefComplaint: Sudden 10/10 'tearing, ripping' chest pain that began instantaneously about 5 minutes before the 911 call while he was sitting at his desk, radiating from the center of his chest straight through to his back between the shoulder blades.

history.hpi: 58-year-old male was sitting at his desk typing when he was struck — with zero warning — by the worst pain of his life. Onset was instantaneous and abrupt: 'I was just sitting here, and BAM!' The quality is NOT pressure — he is emphatic that it is a tearing, ripping feeling unlike anything he has ever felt. It started in the middle of his chest and goes straight through to his back, right between the shoulder blades. Nothing he does makes it better; it hurts to even breathe. Severity is 10/10 — 'the absolute worst.' It started about 5 minutes before his coworker called 911 and has not changed at all since onset. His only medical history is hypertension, for which he takes lisinopril — but he ran out several days ago and has not taken it since. He is pale, sweating profusely, restless, and unable to find a comfortable position.
pastMedical: Hypertension ('just high blood pressure') — currently untreated because he ran out of his medication several days ago
medications: Lisinopril PO daily for blood pressure — ran out; has not taken it in a few days
allergies: None known — 'None that I know of' (NKDA)
history.lastOralIntake: Coffee and a donut about an hour ago
history.events: He was just sitting at his desk, typing, with no warning at all. Instantaneous onset of tearing chest pain radiating through to the interscapular back about 5 minutes before his coworker called 911. No exertion, no trauma, no prodrome.

scene.dispatch: Rescue 5, respond to City Financial Bank at 789 Commerce Street for a 58-year-old male with chest pain. Time out is 07:16.
scene.location: Private office inside City Financial Bank, 789 Commerce Street — ground floor professional office suite. Patient is in his desk chair behind a large desk. Stretcher access is through the lobby and a carpeted hallway; the bank has not yet opened to the public.
scene.time: Weekday morning, 07:16 dispatch; symptom onset approximately 07:10
scene.safety: The scene is a professional office inside a bank. The scene is safe, and there are no immediate hazards. Standard BSI. A coworker ushers the crew into the office where the patient is located.
scene.bystanders: The coworker who called 911 leads the crew in and reports the patient suddenly cried out about five minutes before the call and 'has not looked right since.' No family on scene; the coworker can relay very little medical history — the patient himself is the historian.
visualCues: Middle-aged man sitting in his desk chair, acutely ill in appearance
Pale and sweating profusely — visible beads on his forehead, shirt collar damp
Clutching the center of his chest with one hand
Restless — shifting constantly in the chair, unable to find a comfortable position
Speaking in short, pained sentences but fully oriented
No cyanosis, no obvious trauma, work environment orderly
A wastebasket, keyboard, and coffee cup undisturbed — this hit him out of nowhere mid-task

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: EMS finds a 58-year-old man in agonizing distress with the classic dissection story told almost word for word: instantaneous onset while at rest, a TEARING/RIPPING quality he insists is not pressure, radiation from mid-chest straight through to the interscapular back, 10/10 and unchanged, in a hypertensive patient who stopped his lisinopril days ago. He is A&Ox4, patent airway, breathing fast but not labored, with bounding rapid pulses and pale, cool, clammy skin. The crew's exam is where this case is won or lost: blood pressure obtained in BOTH arms reveals 198/110 on the right versus 150/90 on the left — a 48 mmHg systolic differential — and the left radial pulse is palpably weaker than the bounding right. Under MATC guidance this presentation maps to the Back Pain guideline's life-threat screen for aortic dissection (chest pain with back pain, unequal pulses/perfusion) and to the ACS guideline's deferral clause for likely non-cardiac chest pain: aspirin and nitrates are withheld and pain is managed per the Pain Management guideline — at this crew's BLS scope, position of comfort and verbal reassurance, not analgesics. Definitive care is surgical — the correct posture is recognition, minimal scene time, and transport toward an appropriate facility with a specialty destination considered. Every additional minute on scene is myocardium-irrelevant and aorta-critical.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: RR 24 — respirations fast but not labored; lungs clear bilaterally; splints slightly with deep breaths ('it hurts to even breathe')
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Central and peripheral pulses present, rapid, and strong/bounding on the right; LEFT radial present but noticeably weaker than the right; no obvious bleeding; skin pale, cool, and clammy
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Moves all four extremities; no focal deficit; restless, constantly shifting position
otherFindings: BP RIGHT arm 198/110; BP LEFT arm 150/90 — a 48 mmHg systolic differential, found ONLY if the crew assesses both arms
Right radial 120 and bounding; left radial 120 but distinctly weaker
Pain quality: tearing/ripping — 'It's not pressure' — radiating straight through to between the shoulder blades
Onset instantaneous at rest, 10/10, unchanged — not crescendo anginal pain
Risk factor: hypertension, unmedicated for days (ran out of lisinopril)
Under MATC this is 'likely non-cardiac chest pain' → DEFER aspirin and nitrates; comfort measures per Pain Management
SpO2 96% on room air — inside the 94–98% titration target; no routine high-flow oxygen owed
Definitive care is surgical — recognition and rapid transport are the interventions that matter
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: (short, pained sentences) Oh, thank God... you have to help me... It's the worst pain of my life. It happened all at once... a few minutes ago... like something ripped right down my chest. It goes straight through to my back, right between my shoulder blades.

expectedActions.shortAction: Full vitals; assess BP and pulses side-to-side — R 198/110 vs L 150/90
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Back Pain Assessment 2 requires full vital signs including blood pressure and pulse, and the guideline's documentation standard requires assessment of initial and changing perfusion/pulses. Operationalized here as side-to-side comparison, that exam is the only thing that surfaces the 48 mmHg differential and the weaker left radial — the physical finding that separates this call from ACS. Every piece of it is BLS assessment.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Assessment: Obtain vital signs including pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, neurologic status assessment, pulse oximetry, temperature. Key Documentation Elements: Assesses initial and changes in perfusion/pulses.

expectedActions.shortAction: Screen for aortic emergency — tearing chest-to-back pain plus pulse inequality
expectedActions.rationale: The interscapular radiation places this presentation inside the Back Pain guideline's mandatory life-threat screen, which names aortic dissection explicitly and keys on pulse inequality and associated chest pain. The tearing quality plus the pulse/BP asymmetry found in the previous action complete the pattern. Performance measure for this guideline is literally 'Assessment for life-threatening etiology.'
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Assess for life-threatening causes of back pain, which may include: Aortic dissection or ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm: Unequal femoral or distal lower extremity pulses; "Pulsatile" abdominal mass; Associated abdominal pain and/or chest pain; Known history of abdominal aortic aneurysm or dissection. Performance Measures: Assessment for life-threatening etiology.

expectedActions.shortAction: WITHHOLD aspirin — likely non-cardiac chest pain; comfort measures instead
expectedActions.rationale: MATC ACS Inclusion Criteria 3 is the guideline's own off-ramp: patients with likely non-cardiac chest pain and low likelihood of ACS get aspirin and nitrates DEFERRED, with pain managed per the Pain Management guideline. Tearing pain to the back and a 48 mmHg arm-to-arm differential make this that patient. Aspirin PO is a BLS medication — which makes the protocol-grounded decision NOT to give it a squarely BLS expectation, and giving 324 mg of aspirin to a tearing aorta the single most dangerous 'routine' act available on this scene.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Chest Pain/Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS)/ST-segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Some patients will present with likely non-cardiac chest pain and otherwise have a low likelihood of ACS (e.g., blunt trauma to the chest of a child). For these patients, defer the administration of aspirin (ASA) and nitrates per the Pain Management Guideline.

expectedActions.shortAction: Decide LOAD-AND-GO — appropriate facility; consider aortic specialty destination
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Back Pain Treatment c and Key Consideration 3 — transport to an appropriate receiving facility with a specialty destination center considered for suspected aortic emergency. Definitive care is surgical; there is no field intervention that fixes this. The transport decision IS the treatment, and it should be made in the first minutes, not after an exhaustive on-scene secondary.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Provide transport to an appropriate receiving facility. Consider specialty destination centers for conditions such as suspected aortic emergency. Key Considerations: Consider transport to appropriate specialty center if aortic emergency suspected.

expectedActions.shortAction: AED at the patient's side, pads ready — watch for deterioration
expectedActions.rationale: MATC ACS Patient Safety Considerations — this is exactly the high-risk patient the pads language anticipates: severe pain, hemodynamic extremes, and a disease process one step from arrest. At BLS scope the AED is the defibrillator; staging it with the patient with pads ready costs nothing, while retrieving it after a collapse costs minutes of compressions.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Chest Pain/Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS)/ST-segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Patient Safety Considerations: Observe for signs of clinical deterioration: dysrhythmias, chest pain, shortness of breath, decreased level of consciousness/syncope, or other signs of shock/hypotension. Consider placing defibrillator pads on high-risk patients.

expectedActions.shortAction: Oxygen only as needed to SpO2 94–98% — he is 96% on room air
expectedActions.rationale: MATC ACS step 3 gives oxygen to the dyspneic, hypoxemic, or failing patient with a titration target of 94–98%. At 96% on room air he is inside the target band — routine high-flow oxygen is not what the protocol directs. Titrate if he drops.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Chest Pain/Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS)/ST-segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If the patient is dyspneic, hypoxemic, or has obvious signs of heart failure, EMS clinicians should administer oxygen as appropriate with a target of achieving 94–98% saturation.

transitions.condition: Crew recognizes the tearing chest-to-back pain and the 48 mmHg systolic arm-to-arm differential as a likely non-cardiac (aortic) emergency; aspirin and nitrates are deferred per the ACS guideline's non-cardiac clause, and the crew commits to immediate transport with a specialty destination considered — scene time held under 10 minutes.

Crew anchors on 'chest pain = ACS': bilateral BPs are never compared, a lengthy on-scene secondary assessment and non-pertinent history-taking extend scene time past 10 minutes, and aspirin 324 mg PO is administered. Shortly after the aspirin, the patient lets out a cry — his pain suddenly worsens and he becomes much more pale.

phases.name: ASA held; load-and-go
phases.description: The crew got the two decisions that matter right: no aspirin, no lingering. The patient is moved to the stretcher quickly but carefully, kept sitting up in his position of comfort, and wheeled straight through the lobby to the ambulance. What the crew still owes him under MATC at BLS scope is compassionate, non-pharmacologic pain care: position of comfort and verbal reassurance are named options in the Pain Management guideline, and a documented NRS baseline — 10/10 — starts the trend line the receiving team will need. As he settles onto the stretcher, stiller and coached through his breathing, the catecholamine surge eases fractionally and his pressure begins to drift down from its 198 systolic peak on the right. Early notification lets the receiving facility start assembling what this man actually needs — imaging and a surgical decision — before the ambulance is on the ramp.
phases.triggerCondition: The crew recognized tearing chest-to-back pain with a 48 mmHg systolic BP differential as a suspected aortic emergency, withheld aspirin and nitrates under the ACS guideline's likely non-cardiac clause, and committed to immediate transport. The patient is moved to the stretcher sitting up, quickly but carefully, with scene time under 10 minutes.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: RR 22, fast but not labored; lungs remain clear
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Right radial bounding at 112; left radial still present and weaker; skin pale, cool, clammy
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Moves all four; settling slightly now that he is on the stretcher, still restless
otherFindings: BP RIGHT arm 188/106; BP LEFT arm 142/86 — differential persists (~46 mmHg systolic)
Pain still 10/10 — NRS score assessed and documented as the baseline
Position of comfort: sitting up on the stretcher, moved quickly but carefully; verbal reassurance to control anxiety
Scene interval running under 10 minutes; the clock is the co-intervention
Early notification: 'suspected aortic emergency, 48 mmHg arm-to-arm differential'
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: (gripping the stretcher rail) Please... just get me there. It hasn't let up... not even a little. Straight through to my back... it's still tearing.

expectedActions.shortAction: Stretcher in position of comfort (sitting up); verbal reassurance; move quickly but carefully
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Pain Management 4 — position of comfort and verbal reassurance are named non-pharmacologic measures, and at BLS scope they are the pain care this patient is owed. This restless, terrified patient chooses sitting up; fighting him flat adds pain, anxiety, and catecholamines. Smooth, careful movement is part of the packaging.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Non-pharmacologic pain management options include: Placement of the patient in a position of comfort. Verbal reassurance to control anxiety.

expectedActions.shortAction: Pain score assessed and documented — NRS baseline 10/10
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Pain Management 3c and Key Documentation Elements — an adult self-reports on the Numeric Rating Scale, and the initial pain scale assessment belongs in the record. The 10/10 baseline is also part of the clinical picture that sells 'suspected dissection' to the receiving physician.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Determine patient's pain score assessment using standard pain scale. Greater than 12 years old: Self-report scale: Numeric Rating Scale (NRS). Key Documentation Elements: Documentation of initial patient pain scale assessment.

expectedActions.shortAction: Minimize scene time — no further on-scene workup; everything else happens rolling
expectedActions.rationale: MATC ACS Key Considerations — the guideline's scene-time language exists because time-to-intervention drives mortality in chest-pain emergencies, and it applies with even more force when definitive care is an operating room. Any assessment that can happen in a moving ambulance happens in a moving ambulance.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Chest Pain/Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS)/ST-segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Key Considerations: Acute coronary syndrome may present with atypical pain, vague or only generalized complaints. Ischemic burden time is a risk for morbidity and mortality, EMS can help decrease first medical contact to intervention time/reflow by efficient scripting/training of safely minimizing scene time.

expectedActions.shortAction: Early radio notification — suspected aortic emergency with BP differential
expectedActions.rationale: MATC ACS step 11 — early notification of the patient's condition to the receiving facility. For a suspected aortic emergency that call is what puts imaging and the surgical decision-makers in motion before arrival; a clear report of the tearing story and the arm-to-arm differential changes what the ED does in the first five minutes.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Chest Pain/Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS)/ST-segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Early notification to receiving facility of any changes in patient condition or serial EKGs.

transitions.condition: Patient packaged on the stretcher sitting up in his position of comfort with verbal reassurance given, early notification delivered, and the ambulance rolling toward the receiving facility — total scene interval under 10 minutes.

phases.name: Packaged; en route
phases.description: En route, non-pharmacologic care does what it can: sitting up in his position of comfort, coached breathing, and steady reassurance leave him calmer and stiller, and with the sympathetic surge fractionally blunted his right-arm pressure drifts down from 198 to 172 systolic. His pain remains severe — 9/10 — and the differential persists; it is a structural finding, and nothing in a BLS bag fixes it. The crew's job now is disciplined reassessment: vitals and response to interventions throughout transport, serial NRS pain scores recorded with repeat vitals, and eyes on him for any sign of deterioration — sudden pain change, syncope, signs of shock. Documentation closes the loop: symptom-onset time and — the line item this scenario exists to teach — the reason aspirin was NOT given. Per the source presentation, his condition remains critical but does not deteriorate during transport: the crew gave him the best possible chance by recognizing the emergency and moving.
phases.triggerCondition: Patient packaged sitting up in position of comfort and transport underway within 10 minutes of patient contact. With reassurance and stillness the catecholamine surge eases fractionally — right-arm systolic drifts to the 170s — while pain remains severe and the receiving facility is expecting a suspected aortic emergency.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: RR 18 — slower and more controlled with coaching; still splints with the deepest breaths; lungs clear
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Right radial strong at 104; left radial unchanged — present, weaker; skin pale but no longer dripping
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Moves all four; calmer with reassurance, still guarding his chest
otherFindings: Pain remains severe — 9/10; serial NRS scores documented with repeat vitals
BP RIGHT 172/96; BP LEFT 130/82 — differential persists (~42 mmHg systolic); it is structural
Position of comfort held; reassurance is the analgesia in scope — and it is helping him hold still
No new neuro deficit; mentation intact
Watching for deterioration: worsening pain, syncope, signs of shock
Documentation owed: symptom onset 07:10 and the REASON aspirin was not given
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: (quieter, still gripping the rail) Holding still helps... a little. It's still there — still tearing, straight through to my back. How much longer? Please tell them I'm coming.

expectedActions.shortAction: Reassess vitals and response to interventions throughout transport
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Back Pain Treatment d — reassessment throughout transport is the surveillance net for a disease that can extend or rupture at any moment. Bilateral pressures, pulse symmetry, mentation, and pain score are the specific things worth trending here — all of it BLS assessment.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Reassess vital signs and response to therapeutic interventions throughout transport.

expectedActions.shortAction: Serial NRS pain scores documented with repeat vitals through transport
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Pain Management Key Documentation Elements — reassessment with repeat vital signs and a repeat pain scale score is the documented evidence of serial evaluation. In a dissection the trend line — pain, pressures, pulse symmetry, mentation — is the story the receiving team needs.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Key Documentation Elements: Documentation of patient reassessment with repeat vital signs and patient pain scale assessment.

expectedActions.shortAction: Watch for deterioration — worsening pain, syncope, signs of shock
expectedActions.rationale: MATC ACS Patient Safety Consideration 1 — a dissection can extend or rupture mid-transport and declare itself with a sudden pain change, pre-syncope, or shock. Deliberate deterioration-watching — mentation, skin, pulse symmetry, repeat pressures — is how a BLS crew catches the disease changing shape in time to update the hospital.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Chest Pain/Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS)/ST-segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Patient Safety Considerations: Observe for signs of clinical deterioration: dysrhythmias, chest pain, shortness of breath, decreased level of consciousness/syncope, or other signs of shock/hypotension.

expectedActions.shortAction: Document onset time and the reason aspirin was NOT given
expectedActions.rationale: MATC ACS Key Documentation Elements — the guideline explicitly anticipates the withheld-aspirin case: the record must state the time ASA was given OR the reason it was not. 'Suspected aortic emergency — tearing pain, 48 mmHg arm-to-arm differential' is that reason, in writing.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Chest Pain/Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS)/ST-segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Key Documentation Elements: The time of symptom onset. The time aspirin (ASA) administered, or reason why not given.

expectedActions.shortAction: Transport in position of comfort; reassess pain on arrival at destination
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Pain Management 10 — position of comfort through transport, with a final pain score recorded on arrival to complete the serial documentation set.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Transport in position of comfort and reassess as indicated.

phases.name: ASA given; scene prolonged
phases.description: The crew read 'chest pain' and ran the ACS play from memory: a long on-scene secondary assessment, non-pertinent questions, no second-arm blood pressure — and 324 mg of chewed aspirin. Shortly after the aspirin goes in, the patient lets out a cry; his pain suddenly worsens and he goes much more pale. Scene time is past 10 minutes and the physiology is now moving: heart rate climbing through the 130s, right-arm systolic FALLING from 198 to 158 — a falling pressure in a hypertensive dissection patient is not improvement, it is leaking — and the left radial is now barely palpable. He says the words that should ice every spine in the room: 'I feel very dizzy...' This phase is the last exit. What MATC still offers at BLS scope: recognize the deterioration for what it is, assess for shock per the Back Pain guideline, get the AED pads on a patient who is about to arrest, and move NOW — abandon everything on scene that is not the stretcher. What no protocol offers: a way to take the aspirin back.
phases.triggerCondition: Crew anchored on ACS: no bilateral BP comparison, a lengthy on-scene secondary assessment, and aspirin 324 mg PO administered. Shortly after the aspirin, the patient cries out — pain abruptly worsens, he becomes much more pale, and scene time passes 10 minutes.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: RR 28 and shallowing; no longer just pain-splinting — he is air hungry
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Right radial rapid and weakening from bounding; LEFT radial barely palpable; cap refill 3 sec; skin much more pale, cold, soaked
clinicalPresentation.pupils: Equal at 3 mm, reactive; eyelids heavy
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Still moves all four but has stopped shifting — ominously still now
otherFindings: Aspirin 324 mg PO already chewed and swallowed — cannot be taken back
Immediately post-ASA: cried out, pain suddenly worse, much more pale
BP RIGHT falling: 198 → 158 systolic; LEFT arm 104/70 and barely obtainable — falling pressure here is LEAK, not improvement
HR climbing 120 → 134 — narrowing pulse pressure, rising rate = hemorrhagic trajectory
Patient states: 'I feel very dizzy...' — pre-syncope in this context is pre-arrest
Scene time now exceeds 10 minutes and definitive care is still an OR away
The only correct moves left: AED pads on, shock recognized, wheels moving
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: (a sharp cry as the pain surges) It's worse — something happened — oh God... I feel very dizzy...

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize deterioration — sudden pain change, pallor, dizziness = evolving catastrophe
expectedActions.rationale: MATC ACS Patient Safety Consideration 1 — the guideline's deterioration list reads like this patient's last two minutes: worsening chest pain, decreased level of consciousness/pre-syncope, signs of shock. A falling BP in a patient who was 198 systolic is not 'the aspirin working' — it is volume leaving the circulation.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Chest Pain/Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS)/ST-segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Patient Safety Considerations: Observe for signs of clinical deterioration: dysrhythmias, chest pain, shortness of breath, decreased level of consciousness/syncope, or other signs of shock/hypotension.

expectedActions.shortAction: Assess for shock — falling BP, climbing HR, cold gray skin after sudden pain change
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Back Pain Assessment 6 — the guideline pairs its dissection screen with an explicit shock assessment because rupture is the failure mode. The trend (158 and falling, HR 134 and climbing, left radial vanishing) is the diagnosis; recognition routes care while transport begins.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Assess for signs of shock. If shock is present, provide treatment per appropriate Shock Guideline.

expectedActions.shortAction: AED pads ON now — this patient is peri-arrest
expectedActions.rationale: MATC ACS Patient Safety Consideration 3 — if the AED was not staged earlier, this is the last window to get pads on without pausing compressions to do it. When he arrests, analysis should be seconds away, not a trip back to the truck.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Chest Pain/Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS)/ST-segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Patient Safety Considerations: Consider placing defibrillator pads on high-risk patients.

expectedActions.shortAction: Abort on-scene care; move NOW — appropriate facility, notify en route
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Back Pain Treatment c/d — transport to an appropriate receiving facility with a specialty destination considered, reassessing en route. Every remaining assessment happens rolling. The scene has nothing left to offer this patient; the hospital does.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Provide transport to an appropriate receiving facility. Consider specialty destination centers for conditions such as suspected aortic emergency. Reassess vital signs and response to therapeutic interventions throughout transport.

transitions.condition: At 10–12 minutes of scene time, the patient states 'I feel very dizzy...', his eyes roll back, and he becomes unresponsive. The carotid pulse is absent, blood pressure is unobtainable, and respirations go agonal and then apneic — the aorta has completely ruptured and he is in cardiac arrest.

phases.name: Rupture — cardiac arrest
phases.description: His eyes roll back mid-sentence and he slumps in the chair. No carotid pulse. Blood pressure unobtainable. A few agonal gasps, then apnea. The AED goes on and analyzes: NO SHOCK ADVISED — organized complexes are marching along at 40 with no pulse: PEA, the rhythm of an empty heart. The aorta has completely ruptured; the delay on scene has produced the outcome the load-and-go pathway exists to prevent. The crew now runs the MATC Cardiac Arrest guideline at BLS scope with full understanding of what it can and cannot buy: immediate, minimally interrupted high-quality compressions with rescuers rotating before fatigue; the 2-minute cycle of compressions and rhythm analysis, with compressions continuing through AED analysis-to-charge gaps; an OPA and BVM ventilation delivered so that nothing about the airway interrupts compressions; and resuscitation where he lies, not in a moving ambulance. Debrief honestly: the arrest was not caused by the failure to resuscitate well — it was caused by the aspirin and the ten minutes.
phases.triggerCondition: The patient states 'I feel very dizzy...', his eyes roll back, and he becomes unresponsive. Carotid pulse is absent, BP is unobtainable, and agonal gasps fade to apnea — complete aortic rupture with cardiac arrest, an organized rhythm on the monitor with no pulse (PEA).

clinicalPresentation.airway: Unprotected — no gag, no spontaneous effort; OPA accepted without response
clinicalPresentation.breathing: A few agonal gasps immediately after collapse, now APNEIC; no chest rise without ventilation
clinicalPresentation.circulation: NO carotid pulse; no radial pulses; BP unobtainable; skin gray-white, cold, wet

skin.color: gray-white, mottling beginning at the knees

clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Flaccid — no movement, no response to pain
otherFindings: AED analysis: NO SHOCK ADVISED — organized complexes at ~40/min with NO pulse — PEA; NON-shockable
Witnessed arrest in front of EMS → immediate rhythm analysis, compressions without delay
Compression quality is the whole resuscitation: 100–120/min, 2–2.4 inches, full recoil, rotate rescuers every 2 minutes
Airway is secondary in adult arrest — OPA + BVM, and nothing about it may interrupt compressions
Resuscitate on scene — compressions in a moving ambulance are ineffective and unsafe
Debrief truth: the fatal decisions were the aspirin and the scene time, not the code performance

expectedActions.shortAction: Immediate high-quality compressions — 100–120/min, 2–2.4 inches, full recoil, rotate q2min
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Cardiac Arrest — compressions begin the moment pulselessness is confirmed, and quality is defined numerically: rate, depth, recoil, interruption discipline, and rescuer rotation before fatigue. In PEA from exsanguination, compressions are the only forward flow he has.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Effective chest compressions and defibrillation are the most important therapies to the patient in cardiac arrest. Effective chest compressions are defined as: A rate of greater than 100 and less than 120 compressions/minute. Depth of at least 2 inches (5 cm) and less than 2.4 inches (6 cm) for adults and children or 1.5 inches (4 cm) for infants; adolescents who have entered puberty should receive the same depth of chest compressions as an adult. Allow for complete chest recoil (avoid leaning). Minimize interruptions in compressions. Avoid rescuer fatigue by rotating rescuers at least every 2 minutes.

expectedActions.shortAction: Witnessed arrest: AED on, analyze immediately — no shock advised; 2-minute cycles
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Cardiac Arrest Treatment 1a and 6 — the patient arrested in front of the crew, so rhythm analysis is immediate; the organized-but-pulseless rhythm is PEA, and the AED will advise no shock. The engine of the code is the 2-minute cycle — compressions, analyze, resume — with compressions continuing right up to each analysis.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If adequate, uninterrupted bystander CPR has been performed or if the patient arrests in front of the EMS clinicians, immediately proceed with rhythm analysis and defibrillation, if appropriate. Continue the cycle of chest compressions for 2 minutes, followed by rhythm analysis and defibrillation of shockable rhythms. Continue chest compressions between completion of AED analysis and AED charging.

expectedActions.shortAction: Airway without stopping compressions — OPA + BVM 30:2 or 10/min on the upstroke
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Cardiac Arrest Treatment 6 — in adult arrest, airway management is secondary and must never interrupt compressions. An oropharyngeal airway with upstroke BVM at 10/min, brief-pause 30:2, or initial passive oxygenation all satisfy the guideline at BLS scope; nothing about the airway may cost compression time.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: The airway management strategy should not interrupt compressions. Options for airway management include: Passive ventilation: High flow oxygen is applied via a non-rebreather mask with an oropharyngeal airway. BVM ventilation at 10 breaths per minute (1 breath every 10 compressions), applied during the upstroke between compressions, without interrupting the compressions. BVM ventilation with 30:2 ventilation to compression ratio: Each 30 compressions, the compressions are paused briefly to allow 2 BVM ventilations, then compressions immediately resumed.

expectedActions.shortAction: Work the arrest where he lies — no compressions in a moving ambulance
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Cardiac Arrest Patient Safety Considerations 1–3 — the reflex to 'just go' now inverts: moving degrades compression quality and endangers the crew. The resuscitation happens on scene; the earlier failure to move cannot be repaid by moving badly now.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Performing manual chest compressions in a moving vehicle may pose a clinician safety concern. In addition, manual chest compressions during patient movement are less effective in regard to hands on time, depth, recoil and rate. Ideally, patients should be resuscitated as close to the scene as operationally possible.
